title: A contact path for a consumer brand
metaTitle: A contact path shoppers will finish
excerpt: Say what happens after a shopper writes, how soon, and what to have ready. The action most people need is still to see the product, not a long form.
alt: Clothes on wooden hangers suspended from a white branch against a plain wall. A few pieces, easy to approach, which is how a contact path should feel.

faqs.question: What should a brand contact page tell people?
faqs.answer: Who replies, how soon, and what the reply will contain: a product link, a return step, or a lead time. If a making holiday means silence, print the dates. A fast promise you break teaches people the shop is a costume.

faqs.question: How many fields does a first question need?
faqs.answer: Name, email, which product or order, and a message that can be one line. Show the order-number format in the label if people mistype it. Ask for an account when they need history, not when they need to know if a mug fits a standard machine.

faqs.question: When should contact be split into paths?
faqs.answer: When faults, wholesale, and press go to different people. Name those paths, and make the order question the default. A shopper who does not know you yet should not have to scan past a wholesale pitch to report a chip.

markdown:
A consumer brand contact page should tell a shopper what happens after they reach out, how soon they will hear, and what to have ready. The action most people need is to see the product. A form with ten fields is a way to lose the ones who were ready to look, and often ready to buy.

Contact is the exception. The product page is the main path. Build them in that order or the form will pretend to be the shop.

## Say what happens after they send it

Describe the next step on your side in plain language. A person reads the message. Product questions get a pointer to the right object, or a straight answer about material, timing, or fit. Faults get a repair or a replacement path. Wholesale gets a different reply, with the terms or a refusal. One address can work if a human will route it. If nobody routes it, publish the separate paths and name them.

Say who replies. "You will hear from the person who handles orders" is fair only if it is true. Say how soon, in the terms you keep. Within two working days. During a drop, within four. If a making holiday means silence, say the dates. An honest slower promise beats a fast one you break, because the shopper is deciding whether you are a real shop.

Say what the reply contains. A link to the product that matches the question. A return label, if that is the policy. A lead time for repair. People tolerate a wait when the shape of the answer is printed. Silence reads as a brand that only speaks before the payment.

The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) expect forms to be operable and understandable, with labels that persist and controls that assistive technology can name. Placeholder-only fields fail that, and they fail everyone else when the hint vanishes as they type. Put the label above the field and leave it there. Errors should say what to fix, next to the field, and the text they already entered should remain.

## What to have ready

Ask for the facts that let you answer once. For a product question: which object, in the name the shop uses. For a fault: the order number and what happened, in a sentence, plus a photograph if they have one. For wholesale: the shop name and the city. For a gift: the date they need it, so you can say whether the make time fits.

Do not ask for a life story, a password, and a list of preferences before you have helped. Those belong to an account, created when there is a reason. A first hello that feels like an application will lose the shopper who had a simple question about the glaze. Some will complete anything. The ones you have not yet earned will not.

If a return needs the item unused, say that beside the form, in the same words as the product page. Contradictory rules between contact and product are how a careful brand starts a fight with its own customer. One policy, linked, and a one-line version in both places.

Publish a non-form path. An email address in text, if a person reads it. A postal address for returns, if returns are postal. "See the product" above the fold of the contact page, for the people who arrived here because they could not find the shop. Many contact visits are failed product visits. Fix that by putting the product in reach before you ask anyone to write.

## A form short enough for a phone

Four fields is enough for most notes. Name. Email. Which product or order. A message that can be one line. Mark the message required only when you truly cannot answer without it. An order number field can appear when they chose "fault" or "return," and stay hidden otherwise. Conditional fields respect the errand.

Show the product path above the form. See the product. Use the homepage's verb. A shopper who finds the mug from the contact page and never sends the form is a success. Their question was the mug. The form was a wrong turn you made easy to leave.

Confirm the send on the page. "Message sent. Expect a reply within two working days." Offer the product link again so the confirmation is not a dead end. If the send fails, say so in the brand's voice and keep the draft. Spam checks should be passable on the first try with one hand. A puzzle that defeats the customer defeats the sale you might have saved.

Account walls are a special form of the long form. Let a guest ask a question. Require an account when they need order history, not when they need to know whether the mug fits a standard machine. The answer to that question belongs on the product page anyway. Put it there, and the contact volume will fall.

## Keep the promise operational

A printed reply time is a rota. Decide who watches the inbox, what a sold-out reply looks like, and who covers leave. A good template names the product, answers the limit, and links the live page. A bad template thanks them for joining the family and forgets the question. Store the good template where the next person will find it.

Do not publish a personal mobile number that a maker will resent. Do publish a number if someone will answer during stated hours. "Email is faster" is a useful line when it is true. It sets the path without pretending you run a call center.

Notice, without a theatrical dashboard, whether messages sit. If they sit for a week, change the promise or change the coverage. A brand that photographs care and then ignores the inbox will be described by the inbox, not by the photographs. The contact page is part of the product.

Wholesale and press can have their own short forms so a retailer does not have to write a novel in a general box, and so a shopper's fault report does not sit behind a wholesale pitch. Separate the queues if the volume justifies it. Name them in the menu of the contact page itself: Order question. Wholesale. Press. Three lines. The default is the order question, because that is the shopper who does not know you yet.

## When contact is the wrong door

If the messages mostly ask the price, the material, the size, or the ship date, the earlier pages are incomplete. Put those facts on the product. Measure the improvement in the kind of mail you receive. When the inbox becomes faults, timing, and genuine edge cases, the contact path is doing the right job.

Google's guidance on [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a visitor can leave having done what they came to do. Here the success is either a sent question with a known wait, or a return to the product because the answer was already on the site. A moody "connect" page with no consequence is neither.

Name the menu item Contact or Help. Avoid "Join the conversation." The brand is a shop with objects. The word should sound like a shop. Keep the product link in the header even on this page, so the primary action never disappears.

Separate the queues if more than one kind of message arrives. An order fault, a wholesale pitch, and a press request should not share a single unlabeled box if they go to different people. Three named paths on the contact page are enough: order, wholesale, press. The order path is the default, because that is the shopper who does not know you yet. The others can be quieter links. A retailer can find wholesale. A customer in a hurry should not have to scan past it.

Save the replies that you send more than twice, and store them next to the page. A good reply names the product, states the limit, and links the live object. A reply that restates the manifesto wastes the attention you have left. The customer already wrote. Answer the sentence they wrote.

Put the order number format in the label if your numbers have a shape people mistype. "Order number, printed at the top of your email" prevents a reply that only says we cannot find you. The form should accept a paste from that email without rejecting a space or a lowercase letter. Petty validation is a tax on someone who is already dealing with a fault.

## What the site can stop carrying

Once the doors work, the risk is clutter that flatters the team and delays the object. A manifesto before the product, a journal nobody asked for, a homepage that performs taste. Those cuts are the subject of [what not to put on the site for a consumer brand](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-consumer-brand).

Editing the path from object to a human reply sits inside [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) as a question you can ask of any shop we show. Bring the real inbox, including the questions you are tired of pasting answers to.
